version.approval_notes: Source: attached. Build: Node.js 22+ and python3; in the source folder `npm ci && npm run build`; dist/firefox is the add-on (not minified). It works only with a self-hosted paperus server (https://github.com/qcode-uni-a/paperus) the user connects in the options page; it gets an access token that may only add papers and see which ones the user has. Data goes only to that server, never to the developers. What it does: (1) The toolbar button opens a popup (popup.html) that saves the current page's paper with its PDF, shows the steps, and closes itself; changing the owner there moves a paper it just added (PUT /api/items/{id}/owner). (2) Host permissions https://*/* and http://*/* are requested at install, used only on the user's click or a request from the connected server: to read the clicked page (scripting), fetch its PDF and the supplementary files it links with the user's own access, follow publishers' PDF links that lead through another page or site (ScienceDirect, AIP, Wiley's reader), and reach the user's server. If the user takes the permission back, a button requests it again on a click. (3) Content scripts: arXiv listings and Google Scholar results (include_globs, a domain per country) get a small button per paper; DOIs/arXiv IDs from the page are looked up on the user's server to mark papers the user has, and a click saves one (Scholar: its page opened in a background tab, saved, closed). On the connected server's own pages only, a script registered at runtime relays requests from its Missing page: the extension then opens chosen papers' publisher pages in background tabs (three at once, one per publisher, 90 s each) and saves their PDFs. On a page that lists files or papers (or a Google Scholar profile, whose further pages it fetches like "Show more", at most 1,000 papers), the popup lists them; ticked ones are fetched with the user's access and added (files over 100 MB only when asked again). (4) A log of its steps (page and fetched addresses, answers) is kept in storage.local, shown on the options page, and sent to the user's own server (POST /api/logs) for its administrators. (5) content_security_policy.extension_pages is "script-src 'self'" (Firefox's default without upgrade-insecure-requests): self-hosted servers on a local network are often plain HTTP; the options page warns about that. PRIVACY.md describes all of it.
